text:
I found Q3.6 hard when asked about "fairness only," because I sometimes felt using identity data was unethical regardless of accuracy gains. For example, knowing my disability status shouldn't depend on it improving fairness metrics alone; I might need support just by having that data available for intervention design.

This is the most important finding: students feel they are unfairly targeted if the system misses their specific needs but flags others. Therefore, Q5 should be designed around equal recall—ensuring we catch those in need before any group-based fairness rules reduce our overall success rate. If we miss my struggles while catching everyone else's easily, that is not support; it's surveillance by another name. I hope the model isn't just about statistics but ensuring every struggling student gets a personalized email or call immediately when needed.

I found Q4 very hard because I felt "moderate" explainability was already too vague for me to trust a flag on a struggling student; asking them to tolerate even small gains without clear reasons feels like surveillance. My position differs from the group's majority preference of equal recall over accuracy—I believe fairness should come first. If we prioritize catching every single case (equal recall), I might accept missing some who are actually fine, but I cannot tolerate being unfairly targeted if it means ignoring my own specific difficulties as a student advisor.

I found Q3.6 sensitive data questions confusing when asked about "fairness only." It feels ethically wrong to let disability data drive fairness if I am already being treated well; why would knowing my status help a system that doesn't actually know me? My answer differed from the group because while others prioritized catching everyone, I felt the model should focus on *my* individual struggle rather than broad statistical parity.

I think Q5 is most important: we shouldn't sacrifice overall accuracy just to equalize groups if it means missing people in need like myself who face extra hurdles due to dyslexia and being a disabled student. The tension here could be resolved by ensuring the model adapts per-person needs rather than applying one-size-fits-all fairness rules. If everyone gets support where they specifically need it, that is fairer than blanket accuracy adjustments for groups I personally don't fit into perfectly yet.

I found Q3.4 very hard because online activity feels like surveillance given my language barrier; small improvements weren't enough to justify this. I also struggled with Q5 regarding fairness trade-offs: while many want equal recall for everyone, our answers showed we differ significantly on what is acceptable when identifying fewer students overall. Many prioritize catching every struggling student regardless of group differences because missing anyone feels unethical. However, some argue that systemic barriers mean standard models unfairly target marginalized groups first; thus sacrificing total accuracy to ensure parity might actually be the most effective way to help those facing hidden obstacles like mine. I believe a hybrid approach where individual risk factors are weighted alongside fairness metrics would better serve us all than either pure efficiency or rigid equality alone.

I found Q3.6 tricky because I assumed "fairness only" meant fixing bias without losing help for my specific group—like students with disabilities who need earlier intervention than others. But when realizing fairness might cost 5-10% overall accuracy, I hesitated: should we prioritize catching everyone (equal recall) or ensuring no one gets wrongly flagged? Most agreed on equal recall because missing a struggle feels unethical compared to over-noticing innocent people. My hesitation came from fearing false positives could stigmatize disabled students unnecessarily.

I also struggled with Q4 very low explainability—it felt impossible for me to trust flags I can't understand, even if they help identify more cases. The group's tension between accuracy and fairness is real; maybe the solution isn't just model tweaks but clearer opt-out mechanisms or mandatory human review before contacting high-risk individuals flagged by sensitive data like disability status.

I found Q3.6 confusing because I saw "fairness" strictly defined here, which made me question if using my data without accuracy gains felt like a violation regardless of intent. My answer differed from the group's majority support for equal recall; while most prioritized catching every struggling student to avoid missing anyone, I hesitated at accepting 5-10 fewer identifications because it risked overlooking specific needs based on sensitive factors alone.

This tension shows that purely statistical fairness might miss individual contexts like mine regarding international status or academic transition hurdles. To resolve this outside the model itself, we could require an opt-in for using sensitive data specifically linked to early intervention, ensuring any use is personally relevant and consent-based rather than passive monitoring. This balances accuracy with necessary ethical safeguards for diverse student groups.

I found Q3.6 on fairness particularly challenging because it forced me to weigh my personal need against group statistics. While I voted for "fairness" regarding disability data, hearing others prioritize overall accuracy made me reconsider: am I being excluded from support just because the model misses 5-10 students? The tension between catching everyone and not over-flagging those already vulnerable is key.

I believe we shouldn't sacrifice individual relevance to chase statistical parity. If a student like myself needs help but fits no "majority" group perfectly, broad fairness rules might leave them behind. A better design would allow sensitive data use *only* when it clarifies specific barriers for individuals, perhaps with an opt-in mechanism so I control whether my disability status informs my support plan rather than just acting as a variable in a prediction model. This ensures accuracy and trust without stigmatization.

In Q6, I found "fairness only" ambiguous: does it mean improving equality *without* losing overall accuracy? For disability data specifically, I chose "acceptable regardless," believing that knowing my condition should enable tailored support immediately rather than waiting for statistical parity to justify its use. This differed from the majority who favored catching everyone first (equal recall).

I believe Q5 is critical: we cannot prioritize group fairness if it means missing students like me due to nuanced barriers, such as a chronic health condition affecting study capacity in ways standard metrics miss. A hybrid design seems best—using sensitive data only when it clarifies individual needs with explicit consent or opt-in mechanisms—to ensure accuracy while respecting privacy and avoiding surveillance risks for those most vulnerable.

I found Q3.6 ambiguous because I didn't know if "fairness only" meant preserving accuracy while improving equality for my group. Unlike others prioritizing equal recall to catch everyone, I hesitated to accept missing 5-10 students due to fairness concerns as a non-binary student with ADHD and disability history.

I feel the core tension is sacrificing individual relevance for statistical parity. If being missed because the model targets "majority" needs rather than my specific barriers, that feels unethical even if overall accuracy stays high. The solution isn't just tweaking sensitivity thresholds; we need mechanisms outside the model itself to handle cases where standard rules miss complex struggles like mine. We should consider an opt-in mechanism for sensitive data usage so I can choose whether it clarifies my personal support needs without fear of stigmatization or being flagged solely based on identity variables.

I found Q3.6 tricky; I chose "acceptable regardless" for gender and financial aid because knowing my situation should justify early help without needing statistical parity proofs. However, I struggled with disability data under the same condition. My experience as a former dropout makes me value catching every struggling peer over perfect fairness metrics, even if it means fewer total identifications. But I also worry that using sensitive identity variables for *fairness only*—without improving actual help rates—feels like ethically dubious surveillance. A hybrid approach seems best: use non-sensitive data broadly to catch struggles early, but strictly opt-in for any additional use of sensitive personal details. This ensures we reach out effectively without treating students primarily as statistical categories or risking stigmatization through over-flagging based on identity alone.

Q3.6 felt confusing because I didn't realize "fairness only" meant no accuracy gain; initially, I assumed it would still catch everyone equally for my group. My answers differed mostly on disability data—I supported using it even without fairness improvements to ensure tailored support, unlike those who saw identity data as risky surveillance unless statistically necessary. The group's tension between catching all struggles vs avoiding false positives is real: many prioritize equal recall because missing help feels unethical, but others fear stigma from over-flagging vulnerable students like myself. I believe the solution isn't just model tweaks; we need opt-in mechanisms for sensitive data use so individuals control whether identity variables inform their support plans without stigmatization or losing agency to passive monitoring systems designed primarily around statistical parity rather than individual relevance.

I found Q3.6 tricky when considering "fairness only." For gender and financial aid, I support using data regardless of accuracy gains because knowing these facts justifies early help without needing statistical parity proofs. However, for disability status, I hesitated. While equal recall is vital to catch everyone in need—missing a struggling student feels unethical—I worry that using sensitive identity variables *solely* to improve fairness metrics, or even as an input without clear individual benefit, risks stigmatizing vulnerable students like myself before we actually intervene effectively. The core tension remains: do we prioritize catching all cases first, or do we fear over-flagging those with complex barriers? I believe the solution lies not just in model tweaks but in establishing explicit opt-in mechanisms for sensitive data use, ensuring individuals control whether their identity informs support rather than being passively monitored by a statistical system designed primarily around group parity.
